position: attributive only — before a noun: *the pharmaceutical industry*
contrast: The plural noun *pharmaceuticals* means the drugs themselves: *Sales of pharmaceuticals rose 8 percent*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with making and selling medicines.
examples: She works for a big *pharmaceutical* company in New Jersey.
*Pharmaceutical* research takes years before a drug reaches the market.
The country's *pharmaceutical* industry employs thousands of chemists.

senses.gloss: Extremely good or extremely great.
examples: Her memory is *phenomenal* — she never writes anything down.
The band had *phenomenal* success with its first album.
That was the most *phenomenal* comeback I have ever seen.

senses.gloss: Giving money and help to people in need, or connected with that kind of giving.
examples: The museum depends on *philanthropic* donations.
He spent his last years on *philanthropic* work in West Africa.
The foundation's aims are entirely *philanthropic*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the Philippine government*
contrast: *Philippine* describes the country and its things; a person from the Philippines is *Filipino* (a man, or people in general) or *Filipina* (a woman): *Filipino food*, *a Filipina nurse*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or coming from the Philippines.
examples: The *Philippine* government announced new tariffs on rice.
We flew over the *Philippine* Sea on the way to Manila.
*Philippine* exports of coconut oil have doubled since 2010.

senses.gloss: Having to do with philosophy, or with the big questions about life.
examples: The book raises deep *philosophical* questions about free will.
Their disagreement was *philosophical* rather than practical.

senses.gloss: Calm about a disappointment, because you accept that such things happen.
examples: He is surprisingly *philosophical* about losing the election.
She has grown more *philosophical* about rejection over the years.

contrast: The *g* is silent in the noun *phlegm* (FLEM) but it is pronounced in *phlegmatic*.

senses.gloss: Calm and slow to get excited or upset.
examples: He stayed *phlegmatic* while everyone else panicked.
Her *phlegmatic* manner makes her good in a crisis.
The coach is more *phlegmatic* than any of his players.

form: from *phobia*; also the end of compounds: *claustrophobic*, *arachnophobic*

senses.gloss: Having an overwhelming, unreasonable fear of something.
examples: She is *phobic* about needles and won't look at the nurse.
I get a little *phobic* in crowded elevators.
He is more *phobic* about flying than he likes to admit.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the sounds of speech, or spelled the way it sounds.
examples: Each entry gives a *phonetic* spelling next to the word.
The *phonetic* alphabet helps pilots spell names over the radio.
Finnish spelling is almost completely *phonetic*.

contrast: American spelling is *phony*; British books write *phoney*. It is also a noun for the person: *He's a total phony*.

senses.gloss: Not real, and made to fool people.
examples: He got into the bar with a *phony* ID.
The check turned out to be *phony*.

senses.gloss: Pretending to feel something; insincere.
examples: She gave me a *phony* smile and walked away.
His apology sounded even *phonier* than his excuse.

senses.gloss: Looking good in photographs.
examples: Her brother is annoyingly *photogenic*.
It's a *photogenic* little town with a harbor and white houses.
She is far more *photogenic* than she thinks.

senses.gloss: Having to do with photography or photographs.
examples: The library keeps a *photographic* record of the whole street.
He brought his *photographic* equipment in two heavy cases.

senses.gloss: So exact that it is like a photograph — said of memory.
examples: She has an almost *photographic* memory for faces.
His recall of the license plate was practically *photographic*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *photovoltaic cells*

senses.gloss: Turning sunlight directly into electricity.
examples: The roof is covered with *photovoltaic* panels.
*Photovoltaic* cells have gotten much cheaper in ten years.
The company builds *photovoltaic* systems for warehouses.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a phrasal verb*

senses.gloss: Made of a group of words that work together as one unit — a grammar term.
examples: *Give up* and *run into* are *phrasal* verbs.
The chapter on *phrasal* verbs is the longest in the book.
Dictionaries list *phrasal* verbs under the main verb.

contrast: In American English *a physical* is also a noun — a medical checkup: *I have my annual physical on Friday*.

senses.gloss: Of the body rather than the mind.
examples: The job takes a lot of *physical* strength.
He is in great *physical* shape for sixty.

senses.gloss: Existing as a real thing you can touch.
examples: There is no *physical* evidence linking him to the scene.
Some readers still prefer a *physical* book to a screen.

senses.gloss: Involving a lot of rough contact or force.
examples: It was a *physical* game, with fouls on both sides.
This league is much more *physical* than the one he came from.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the way the body works.
examples: Stress produces real *physiological* changes, not just feelings.
The drug has a *physiological* effect within minutes.
The cause of the tremor turned out to be *physiological*.

senses.gloss: Kept in vinegar or salt water so that it does not spoil.
examples: She served the sandwiches with *pickled* onions.
*Pickled* herring is a holiday dish in his family.
The beets on the salad bar are *pickled*, not fresh.

senses.gloss: Hard to please, especially about food or small details.
examples: My son is a *picky* eater who lives on pasta.
She is very *picky* about who she works with.
He got *pickier* the longer the apartment search went on.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a pictorial history*

senses.gloss: Using pictures, or told in pictures.
examples: It's a *pictorial* history of the railroad in fifty photographs.
The shelf comes with a *pictorial* guide instead of instructions.
The magazine ran a *pictorial* essay on the flood.

senses.gloss: Pretty in an old-fashioned way that would make a good picture.
examples: They stayed in a *picturesque* village in Vermont.
The harbor is the most *picturesque* part of town.
The old mill is *picturesque* but falling apart.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a piddling amount*

senses.gloss: So small that it is not worth bothering about.
examples: They offered a *piddling* raise after three years.
We argued for an hour over a *piddling* sum of money.
He wasted the whole afternoon on *piddling* details.

form: compound — *piece* + old *-meal* (a bit at a time)
contrast: *Piecemeal* is also an adverb, with no *-ly*: *The reforms were introduced piecemeal*.

senses.gloss: Done a bit at a time, without an overall plan.
examples: The repairs were done in a *piecemeal* way over ten years.
Congress passed a *piecemeal* set of fixes instead of one bill.
Their approach to the housing shortage has been *piecemeal* at best.

senses.gloss: Having a small hole made in it on purpose, usually for jewelry.
examples: She has *pierced* ears and wears tiny gold hoops.
His left ear is *pierced*, but he leaves it empty at work.
Only one of the twins has *pierced* ears.

contrast: *A piercing* is also a noun — the hole itself or the ring in it: *She has three piercings*.

senses.gloss: So loud and high that it hurts to hear.
examples: A *piercing* whistle stopped the game.
The smoke alarm was *piercing* enough to wake the neighbors.

senses.gloss: Sharp and cold enough to go right through you.
examples: A *piercing* wind came off the lake.
The cold was even more *piercing* at the top of the hill.

senses.gloss: Looking at you so sharply that it feels uncomfortable.
examples: He has *piercing* blue eyes.
She gave me a *piercing* look over her glasses.

senses.gloss: Stubborn in a stupid way, refusing to change your mind.
examples: He is too *pigheaded* to ask for directions.
Her *pigheaded* refusal to sign cost them the deal.
Of the two brothers, the younger one is more *pigheaded*.

senses.gloss: Slightly pink.
examples: The sky turned a *pinkish* gray just after sunset.
She wore a *pinkish* scarf over a white shirt.
The meat is still *pinkish* in the middle.

senses.gloss: Having a pattern of very thin stripes, usually on a dark suit.
examples: He showed up in a *pinstriped* suit and a red tie.
The bank's lawyers were all in *pinstriped* gray.
Her jacket is navy and lightly *pinstriped*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a pint-sized kitchen*

senses.gloss: Very small — often said with affection about children.
examples: Her *pint-sized* brother beat everyone at chess.
They live in a *pint-sized* apartment near campus.
The store sells *pint-sized* versions of all its tools.

senses.gloss: Deeply religious.
examples: Her grandmother was the most *pious* person in the family.
He comes from a *pious* farming family in rural Ohio.

senses.gloss: Sounding moral in a way that annoys people.
examples: Spare me the *pious* lecture about hard work.
The speech was full of *pious* talk and no real plan.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste.
examples: The sauce is *piquant* without being hot.
He served a *piquant* salad of arugula and lemon.

senses.gloss: Interesting in a lively, slightly sharp way.
examples: There is a *piquant* detail in the last paragraph.
The story is made more *piquant* by the fact that they were neighbors.

position: predicative only — before a noun Americans use *pissed-off*: *a pissed-off customer*
contrast: Rude and informal. In British English *pissed* means *drunk*; Americans say *wasted* or *hammered* for that.

senses.gloss: Informal and rude: angry.
examples: She was really *pissed* at me for forgetting her birthday.
He gets *pissed* about the smallest things.
I have never seen him more *pissed* than he was that night.

position: both — before a noun it takes a hyphen: *a pissed-off customer*
contrast: Rude but very common in speech. *Pissed* alone means the same thing in American English, but *drunk* in British English.

senses.gloss: Informal and rude: annoyed or angry.
examples: He is *pissed off* because nobody told him about the meeting.
Don't call her now — she is still *pissed off* at her boss.
The longer the bus took, the more *pissed off* the crowd got.

senses.gloss: Completely black, with no light at all.
examples: It was *pitch-black* in the hallway when the power went out.
She has *pitch-black* hair and pale skin.
We drove home down a *pitch-black* country road.

senses.gloss: So dark that you cannot see anything at all.
examples: By six o'clock in December it is already *pitch-dark*.
We felt our way along the *pitch-dark* tunnel.
The cabin was *pitch-dark* and freezing when we got there.

senses.gloss: Short and full of meaning.
examples: He answered with a *pithy* line that everyone quoted afterward.
Her advice is always *pithy*: do the hard part first.
The second draft is *pithier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Making you feel sorry; sad to see.
examples: The dog gave a *pitiful* whine at the door.
The families arrived at the border in a *pitiful* state.

senses.gloss: So bad or so small that it deserves contempt.
examples: They offered a *pitiful* amount of money for the house.
His second excuse was even more *pitiful* than the first.

senses.gloss: So important that everything turns on it.
examples: The election was a *pivotal* moment in the country's history.
She played a *pivotal* role in getting the law passed.
His testimony was *pivotal* in winning the case.

senses.gloss: Calm and not easily upset.
examples: The older mare is more *placid* than the young one.
He has a *placid* temperament that nothing seems to shake.

senses.gloss: Still and quiet — of water or a scene.
examples: The lake was *placid* that morning.
They rowed across *placid* water to the island.

contrast: The noun *plain* (a wide flat stretch of land) and the noun *plane* (an airplane) sound the same. In *That's just plain wrong*, *plain* is an adverb meaning *completely*.

senses.gloss: Easy to see or understand; obvious.
examples: It was *plain* to everyone that she didn't want to go.
Let me make one thing *plain*: I am not paying for it.

senses.gloss: Simple, with nothing added or decorated.
examples: I'll have a *plain* bagel with butter.
The *plainer* the design, the better it ages.

senses.gloss: Not especially good-looking.
examples: She thought of herself as *plain*, which she wasn't.
It's a *plain* little house on a very nice street.

senses.gloss: Saying what you think in simple, direct words.
examples: Voters liked him because he was *plainspoken*.
She is a *plainspoken* woman who flatters nobody.
He is more *plainspoken* than most politicians dare to be.

senses.gloss: Sounding sad, like a complaint or a cry.
examples: A *plaintive* violin played in the background.
The kitten made a *plaintive* sound under the porch.
Her voice grew more *plaintive* with every question.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *planetary orbits*

senses.gloss: Having to do with planets, or with the whole planet.
examples: The telescope studies *planetary* atmospheres.
Scientists describe the ice melt as a *planetary* emergency.
The museum has a *planetary* model hanging in the lobby.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive verb: *The trip was planned months ago*

senses.gloss: Decided on and arranged in advance.
examples: The *planned* shutdown will last two days.
Half of the *planned* housing was never built.
A *planned* city like Brasília looks nothing like an old one.

position: both — the *drunk* sense comes after a verb: *He got plastered*

senses.gloss: Informal: very drunk.
examples: He got *plastered* at the office party.
Half the wedding guests were *plastered* by nine o'clock.

senses.gloss: Stuck flat to a surface, or covered all over with something.
examples: His hair was *plastered* to his forehead by the rain.
The wall was *plastered* with old concert posters.

contrast: Written with a small *p* for friendship; a capital *P* means the philosopher Plato: *Platonic philosophy*.

senses.gloss: Close but not sexual — of a friendship.
examples: They insist their relationship is purely *platonic*.
He wanted more than a *platonic* friendship.
Their love stayed *platonic* for forty years.

senses.gloss: Reasonable enough to be believed, even if it may not be true.
examples: That is the only *plausible* explanation I have heard.
His story sounds *plausible* until you check the dates.
The second theory is more *plausible* than the first.

senses.gloss: In good enough condition to play a game on, or to play through.
examples: The field is *playable* again after all that rain.
The demo is rough, but it's *playable*.

senses.gloss: Easy enough for a musician to actually play.
examples: He arranged the piece so that it is *playable* by beginners.
The part is barely *playable* at that tempo.

position: both — before a noun it takes a hyphen: *a played-out formula*

senses.gloss: No longer fresh or interesting; used up.
examples: That joke is completely *played out*.
The style was *played out* by the time it reached the mall.
By the fourth season the show felt *played out*.

senses.gloss: Full of fun, and not meant seriously.
examples: The younger dog is much more *playful* than the old one.
She gave him a *playful* shove.
His tone was *playful*, but the question was real.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a pleading look*

senses.gloss: Showing that you are begging for something.
examples: She gave me a *pleading* look across the table.
There was a *pleading* note in his voice.
He held up his hands in a *pleading* gesture.

senses.gloss: Nice and enjoyable.
examples: We had a *pleasant* evening on the porch.
The weather was *pleasant* all week.

senses.gloss: Friendly and polite — of a person.
examples: The woman at the desk was very *pleasant*.
He is more *pleasant* to deal with than his partner.

contrast: *Pleasurable* describes the thing that gives pleasure and sounds more formal than *pleasant* or *enjoyable*: *a pleasurable experience*, not *a pleasurable man*.

senses.gloss: Giving a feeling of pleasure.
examples: A long swim is one of the most *pleasurable* things I know.
The wine made the meal even more *pleasurable*.
She found the work slow but oddly *pleasurable*.

contrast: Usually said with a sneer, or as a joke about yourself. It is also a noun for an ordinary citizen of ancient Rome.

senses.gloss: Common or low-class.
examples: He called their taste in music *plebeian*.
My *plebeian* tastes run to hot dogs and cheap beer.
Nothing, she said, could be more *plebeian* than a paper plate.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a plenary session*

senses.gloss: Attended by all the members of a group.
examples: The report will be presented at Friday's *plenary* session.
Delegates met in a *plenary* meeting on the last day.

senses.gloss: Complete and without limits — of power or authority.
examples: The governor claimed *plenary* authority over the budget.
The board has *plenary* power to fire the director.

senses.gloss: Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
examples: Rain was *plentiful* that summer.
Jobs were more *plentiful* before the plant closed.
The region has a *plentiful* supply of cheap electricity.

senses.gloss: Easy to bend without breaking.
examples: Warm the leather until it is *pliable*.
Young branches are more *pliable* than old ones.

senses.gloss: Easy to influence or control — of a person.
examples: They wanted a *pliable* judge on the case.
New recruits are young and *pliable*.

senses.gloss: Slow, heavy and dull.
examples: The movie has a *plodding* first hour.
He works at a *plodding* but reliable pace.
The sequel is even more *plodding* than the original.

senses.gloss: Brave, especially when you are small or the odds are against you.
examples: The *plucky* underdogs took the game to overtime.
She was a *plucky* kid who never backed down.
No team in the tournament was *pluckier*.

contrast: A kind word for *fat*, used of babies, cheeks, chickens and cushions — not an insult the way *fat* is.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly round and full.
examples: He has *plump* cheeks and a wide smile.
Choose the *plumpest* tomatoes in the box.
The cat has gotten *plump* over the winter.

contrast: *Plural* is also a noun: *The plural of "child" is "children"*.

senses.gloss: Showing more than one — a grammar term.
examples: *Mice* is the *plural* form of *mouse*.
The verb has to agree with a *plural* subject.
In this dialect the ending is *plural*, not possessive.

senses.gloss: Made up of many different groups, beliefs or cultures living side by side.
examples: The United States is a *pluralistic* society by design.
They argue for a more *pluralistic* press.
The country's politics have become genuinely *pluralistic*.

position: both — before a noun (*a plus factor*) and right after a letter grade (*a B plus*)
contrast: *Plus* is usually a preposition (*two plus two*) or a noun (*That's a real plus*). As an adjective it lives in a few set phrases: *a plus factor*, *plus sizes*, *a B plus*.

senses.gloss: Slightly above the letter grade named.
examples: She got a B *plus* on the essay.
A C *plus* was not going to save his average.

senses.gloss: Extra, or above the usual amount.
examples: Fluent Spanish is a *plus* factor for anyone applying.
The store carries a full range of *plus* sizes.

senses.gloss: Expensive and very comfortable.
examples: They stayed in a *plush* hotel downtown.
His new office is *plusher* than the one he had before.

senses.gloss: Made of a soft, thick fabric.
examples: She sleeps with a *plush* rabbit.
The seats were covered in *plush* red velvet.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a pneumatic drill*
contrast: The *p* is silent: *pneumatic* begins like *new*.

senses.gloss: Worked by air pressure, or filled with air.
examples: The crew was tearing up the street with a *pneumatic* drill.
The door closes on a *pneumatic* hinge.
*Pneumatic* tires made bicycles comfortable to ride.

ru: варёный без скорлупы, припущенный; добытый браконьером

senses.gloss: Cooked gently in barely boiling liquid.
examples: I'll have two *poached* eggs on toast.
The menu has *poached* salmon with dill.

senses.gloss: Taken by illegal hunting.
examples: Customs seized a shipment of *poached* ivory.
*Poached* rhino horn sells for a fortune in Asia.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a pocket-sized camera*

senses.gloss: Small enough to carry in a pocket.
examples: He keeps a *pocket-sized* notebook for phone numbers.
The museum sells a *pocket-sized* guide to the collection.
It's a *pocket-sized* radio that runs on two batteries.

senses.gloss: Covered with small holes or scars.
examples: The road was *pockmarked* with potholes after the winter.
His face was *pockmarked* from a childhood illness.
We crossed a *pockmarked* stretch of desert.

contrast: *Poetic justice* is a fixed phrase for a punishment that fits perfectly: *It was poetic justice that the thief's car was stolen*.

senses.gloss: Beautiful and full of feeling, like poetry.
examples: His description of the coast is almost *poetic*.
There was something *poetic* about the empty station at dawn.
Her prose is more *poetic* than his.

senses.gloss: Having to do with poetry.
examples: She studies the *poetic* forms of the Renaissance.
The book explains *poetic* meter in plain English.

contrast: The *g* is not pronounced as a separate sound: say POYN-yuhnt.

senses.gloss: Sad and moving in a way that stays with you.
examples: The last scene is quietly *poignant*.
It was a *poignant* moment when the old man stood up to speak.
Her letters are more *poignant* now that we know how it ended.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a point-blank refusal*
contrast: *Point-blank* is also an adverb: *She refused point-blank*, *He was shot at point-blank range*.

senses.gloss: Fired from very close range.
examples: The witness described a *point-blank* shot.
At *point-blank* range even a poor marksman cannot miss.

senses.gloss: Completely direct and blunt.
examples: She gave him a *point-blank* refusal.
It was a *point-blank* question and he could not dodge it.

senses.gloss: Having a sharp end or tip.
examples: The fence has *pointed* iron tops.
He wore a pair of *pointed* black boots.

senses.gloss: Clearly aimed at one person, and usually critical.
examples: She made a *pointed* remark about people who arrive late.
The second question was more *pointed* than the first.

senses.gloss: Having no purpose; not worth doing.
examples: Arguing with him is *pointless*.
They spent the day in *pointless* meetings.
Nothing is more *pointless* than a rule nobody enforces.

position: both — the *ready* sense comes after a verb: *The team is poised to win*

senses.gloss: Ready and about to do something.
examples: The company is *poised* to enter the Asian market.
Troops were *poised* for an attack on the border.

senses.gloss: Calm and confident in the way you carry yourself.
examples: She was remarkably *poised* for a fifteen-year-old.
He is more *poised* on camera than in person.

contrast: Americans call a plant or berry *poisonous* if it harms you when you eat or touch it, and a snake or spider *venomous* if it injects poison by biting.

senses.gloss: Containing poison; able to kill or harm you.
examples: Some *poisonous* mushrooms look exactly like safe ones.
The fumes from the fire were *poisonous*.

senses.gloss: Full of hatred, and damaging to everyone around.
examples: The office had a *poisonous* atmosphere for months.
The debate got more *poisonous* every week.

contrast: American spelling is *poky*; British writing often has *pokey* for the cramped meaning.

senses.gloss: Annoyingly slow.
examples: We got stuck behind a *poky* old truck.
My laptop gets *pokier* every year.

senses.gloss: Small and cramped.
examples: They rented a *poky* apartment above the store.
The kitchen is *poky*, but it works.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *polar ice*

senses.gloss: Having to do with the North or South Pole.
examples: *Polar* bears are losing the ice they hunt on.
The ship was built for *polar* waters.

senses.gloss: Completely opposite — in the phrase *polar opposite*.
examples: The two brothers are *polar* opposites.
Her approach is the *polar* opposite of his.

senses.gloss: Strongly attacking or defending an opinion.
examples: The essay is *polemical* rather than balanced.
He wrote a *polemical* book about the war.
Her later articles are more *polemical* than her early ones.

senses.gloss: Rubbed until it shines.
examples: The hallway has *polished* wooden floors.
His shoes were *polished* to a shine.

senses.gloss: Done with great skill, with no rough edges left.
examples: It was a *polished* performance from a young actor.
His second draft is much more *polished*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with government and the fight for power.
examples: She says she has no *political* ambitions.
The decision was *political*, not economic.

senses.gloss: Interested in politics, or maneuvering for advantage inside a group.
examples: He became *political* in college.
The department got more *political* after the merger.

contrast: Often shortened to *PC*, and usually said with disapproval: *That's a very PC way to put it*.

senses.gloss: Careful to use language and ideas that will not offend any group.
examples: The company put out a carefully *politically correct* statement.
He complains that campuses are too *politically correct*.
The new textbooks are more *politically correct* than the ones I had.

senses.gloss: Likely to offend a group of people, sometimes on purpose.
examples: He tells *politically incorrect* jokes at every family dinner.
The novel is deliberately *politically incorrect*.
Her stand-up act is the most *politically incorrect* thing on TV.

senses.gloss: Made dirty and unsafe by chemicals, smoke or waste.
examples: The river is too *polluted* to swim in.
They live in one of the most *polluted* cities in the world.
*Polluted* groundwater turned up under the old plant.

form: -ish from *Pollyanna*, the endlessly cheerful girl in a 1913 novel
contrast: Always a criticism: it says the optimism ignores the facts.

senses.gloss: Cheerfully optimistic in a way that ignores real problems.
examples: His forecast struck the board as *Pollyannaish*.
I don't want to sound *Pollyannaish*, but I think we'll be fine.
The report is more *Pollyannaish* than the numbers allow.

senses.gloss: Having more than one husband or wife at the same time.
examples: The sect was openly *polygamous* until the 1890s.
He grew up in a *polygamous* household.
*Polygamous* marriage is illegal in all fifty states.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a polyglot city*
contrast: *Polyglot* is also a noun for a person who speaks many languages: *She's a polyglot — five languages*.

senses.gloss: Using or containing many languages.
examples: Queens is a *polyglot* borough where over a hundred languages are spoken.
The firm has a *polyglot* staff and clients on four continents.
He put together a *polyglot* edition of the poem.

contrast: Also a noun for a person: *She's Polynesian on her mother's side*.

senses.gloss: From the islands of Polynesia in the central Pacific.
examples: The museum has a room of *Polynesian* carvings.
*Polynesian* navigators crossed the Pacific in canoes.
Much of the island's music is *Polynesian* in origin.

senses.gloss: Believing in many gods.
examples: Ancient Greek religion was *polytheistic*.
The empire tolerated *polytheistic* worship for centuries.
Hinduism looks *polytheistic* from the outside, though many Hindus disagree.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *polyunsaturated fats*

senses.gloss: Of a fat or oil: of the kind considered better for the heart.
examples: Sunflower oil is high in *polyunsaturated* fat.
The label lists *polyunsaturated* and saturated fats separately.
Doctors recommend *polyunsaturated* oils instead of butter.

senses.gloss: Acting more important than you are, especially in the way you talk.
examples: The speech was long and *pompous*.
He is a *pompous* man who asks to be called *Doctor* at dinner.
Nobody at the table was more *pompous* than the host.

senses.gloss: Heavy and slow-moving.
examples: The elephant turned with *ponderous* dignity.
A *ponderous* truck blocked the whole street.

senses.gloss: Dull and far too serious — of writing or speech.
examples: The book is *ponderous* and could lose a hundred pages.
His lectures are more *ponderous* than his articles.

contrast: *Popular* means liked by many people; *populous* means having many people living there: *the most populous state*, not *the most popular state*.

senses.gloss: Liked by a lot of people.
examples: She is the most *popular* teacher in the school.
The app is especially *popular* with college students.

senses.gloss: Of or for ordinary people; general.
examples: He won the *popular* vote but lost the election.
*Popular* opinion has shifted on the issue.

position: both — almost always with an adverb: *densely populated*, *sparsely populated*

senses.gloss: Lived in by people — normally with a word saying how many.
examples: The coast is densely *populated*.
They moved to a sparsely *populated* part of Montana.
The eastern half of the state is far more *populated* than the west.

contrast: Not *popular*. *Populous* = with many people living there; *popular* = liked by many people.

senses.gloss: Having a large number of people living there.
examples: California is the most *populous* state in the country.
China was the world's most *populous* nation for centuries.
The delta is *populous* and very hard to evacuate.

senses.gloss: Showing sexual acts in a way meant to excite people.
examples: The site was shut down for hosting *pornographic* material.
The court had to decide whether the film was *pornographic*.
He was fired for keeping *pornographic* images on a work computer.

senses.gloss: Full of tiny holes that let liquid or air through.
examples: Sandstone is *porous*, so it soaks up water.
Use a sealer on the *porous* side of the tile.

senses.gloss: Easy to get through or across — of a border or a defense.
examples: The border is long and *porous*.
Their defense got more *porous* in the second half.

contrast: In American schools *a portable* is also a noun — a temporary classroom trailer.

senses.gloss: Light and easy to carry around.
examples: She travels with a *portable* speaker.
The newer machine is smaller and far more *portable*.

senses.gloss: Able to be taken from one job or country to another — of benefits or skills.
examples: His pension is *portable* if he changes employers.
Coding is a *portable* skill.

contrast: A polite, slightly old-fashioned word for a heavy man; it is not used about women. Like *friendly* and *lonely*, it ends in *-ly* but is an adjective.

senses.gloss: Rather fat — usually said of a middle-aged man.
examples: A *portly* gentleman in a vest showed us to our seats.
He has grown *portly* since he stopped playing ball.
The older brother is the *portlier* of the two.

contrast: Also a noun — the language (*She speaks Portuguese*) and the people (*the Portuguese*). The plural has no *-s*: *one Portuguese, two Portuguese*.

senses.gloss: From Portugal, or in the language of Portugal and Brazil.
examples: They ordered a bottle of *Portuguese* wine.
Brazil is the largest *Portuguese*-speaking country.
The tiles on the church are clearly *Portuguese*.

contrast: The word came from British English. Americans use it about expensive places and things (*a posh hotel*), not about a person's accent the way the British do.

senses.gloss: Expensive and elegant.
examples: They had dinner at a *posh* restaurant on the waterfront.
Her new place is a lot *posher* than the old one.
It's a *posh* neighborhood with gates at both ends.

senses.gloss: Good, hopeful, or helpful.
examples: The reviews have been more *positive* than we expected.
Try to stay *positive* about the move.

senses.gloss: Completely sure.
examples: I'm *positive* I locked the door.
Are you *positive* it was him?

senses.gloss: Showing that a substance or an illness is there — of a test.
examples: Her test came back *positive*.
Two players tested *positive* the day before the game.

senses.gloss: Greater than zero, or carrying the charge of a proton.
examples: Multiply the two *positive* numbers first.
Connect the red wire to the *positive* terminal.

position: predicative only — after a verb, or straight after the noun: *he fought like a man possessed*
contrast: *Possessed of* is a formal way of saying *having*: *She is possessed of enormous patience*. Do not confuse it with *possessive*.

senses.gloss: Controlled by an evil spirit, or acting as if you were.
examples: The villagers believed the girl was *possessed*.
He worked like a man *possessed* for three days straight.

senses.gloss: Formal: having a quality or a thing.
examples: She is *possessed* of a sharp memory and a sharper tongue.
The family was *possessed* of a large fortune.
